opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, the first thing I'd say is: respect the spreadsheet. People in tech sometimes look at a race team's workbook and think, "This is a mess, let's replace it." But those spreadsheets are the institutional memory of the team. They've been built up over years by engineers trackside, at 2 a.m., under enormous time pressure. Every odd column, every color code, every tab named "FINAL_v3_USE_THIS" exists for a reason, even if that reason only lives in someone's head.

So the complexity isn't really the formulas. It's the implicit knowledge. A cell might say "+2 clicks" and to a race engineer that means something very specific about a damper setting on a particular car at a particular circuit. A tab might mix setup data, tire degradation notes, and driver feedback all in one grid because that's how the engineer thinks about a session. None of that is labeled for a machine.

When we help teams make that usable by AI, I think about it in three layers. First, structure: can we untangle what's a raw measurement, what's a derived calculation, and what's a human judgment call? Those need to be treated very differently. Second, context: we sit with the engineers and capture the vocabulary, the units, the conventions, basically writing down the stuff they'd teach a new hire over six months. That context is often more valuable to a model than the numbers themselves. And third, trust: the AI has to show its work and point back to the actual cells and sessions it's drawing from, because no engineer will change a setup based on an answer they can't trace.

And the other thing is you don't force them to abandon the spreadsheet. The goal is to meet them where they work. If the model can read and reason over what they already have, and the engineers can see it getting things right, then adoption follows naturally. If you ask them to rebuild their whole workflow mid-season, it's never going to happen.

r001.rationale: It names color codes as part of the spreadsheet’s accumulated complexity, beyond the entered measurements and data.

r002.rationale: It describes making spreadsheets usable by AI and supporting adoption, but does not argue that downstream results justify the investment in conversion.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the first thing I'd say is that the spreadsheets aren't really spreadsheets, they're institutional memory. When you open a race engineer's workbook, you're looking at fifteen years of decisions made under pressure on a Saturday night. There's a tab that nobody remembers creating that still feeds a cell on the main page. There's a column called "corr2" that means something very specific to one person, who may have left the team two seasons ago. So I try very hard not to treat the complexity as a mess to be cleaned up. The complexity is the data. It's where the knowledge lives.

The second thing is that racing teams are unusual in how well-documented their chaos is, even if it isn't documented in a way a machine can read. Every tyre pressure, every ride height change, every weather note has been written down somewhere, because the sport punishes you for forgetting. So the raw material is actually extraordinary. The problem is that it was written for humans who already understood the context, and a model doesn't have that context.

So the way I think about it is in layers. The bottom layer is just structure: can we get this into a shape where a row means one thing and a column means one thing, consistently. That sounds trivial and it's usually the hardest part, because it forces conversations about what the data actually means. The middle layer is the semantics, the glossary, the "corr2 means tyre temperature correction on the second stint" bit. And the top layer is the stuff that never got written down at all, which you only get by sitting next to the engineer and asking why they always ignore the sensor on the rear left in the wet.

What I've learned is that if you skip the middle and top layers and just dump the raw sheets into an AI system, you get something that sounds confident and is wrong in ways that the engineers can spot instantly, and then you've lost them. Trust in a racing garage is very hard to earn back. So I'd rather spend three weeks on the glossary than three days on the model. The AI part, honestly, is the easy bit now. The hard bit is making sure it inherits what the team already knows instead of overwriting it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses hidden tabs, column meanings, and unwritten knowledge, but does not identify highlighting as part of the spreadsheet complexity.

r002.rationale: It says the glossary and context matter for reliable AI, but does not argue that downstream results from converting the data justify the investment.

astra-6.text:
I’d start by asking what the spreadsheet means to the people using it. A sheet can look incredibly complicated, but there may be a clear workflow behind it. The challenge is that some of that logic lives in formulas and labels, and some lives in somebody’s head.

So before bringing AI into it, I’d want to understand what each row represents, what the units are, how the data gets updated, and which version the team trusts. If a colour or a tab name carries meaning, that needs to be made explicit too.

The goal isn’t necessarily to replace their spreadsheets. It’s to preserve the knowledge in them while making the structure and context clear enough that an AI system can use the data reliably—and ask for clarification when it can’t.

r001.rationale: The response says a colour can carry meaning that must be made explicit, identifying spreadsheet highlighting as meaningful context beyond the entered data.

r002.rationale: The response explains preparing data for reliable AI use, but does not argue that downstream results justify the investment in conversion.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to separate the complexity of the spreadsheet from the complexity of what the team is trying to understand. A spreadsheet might look messy, but there may be a lot of expertise embedded in it—in the formulas, the layout, and the assumptions people know without writing them down.

So I’d start by asking the team to walk through how they use it. What does each row represent? What do the units mean? Which values are measured, and which are calculated? Then you can make that context explicit and give the data a consistent structure. The goal is to preserve the team’s knowledge while making it easier for AI to interpret reliably.

r001.rationale: The response mentions formulas, layout, and unwritten assumptions, but does not identify highlighting as part of the spreadsheets’ complexity.

r002.rationale: It says structuring the data helps AI interpret it reliably, but does not argue that downstream results justify the investment in conversion.
